primary_source.title: Lasting recognition of threatening people by wild American crows

review_method: Marzluff et al. (2010) read in full. Trapping and banding 7 wild crows on university campus using rubber caveman mask; recorded mobbing response rates from wild and naive crows over 5 years. Spreading of threat response through social learning and horizontal/vertical transmission verified.

claims.paraphrase: In Seattle, researchers wearing a rubber caveman mask trapped and banded seven wild crows and set them free.
claims.printed_page_locator: Animal Behaviour 79(3), pp. 699-701, Methods: Trapping and dangerous face conditioning
claims.support_summary: Researchers trapped 7 crows with net launcher while wearing a caveman mask; crows were banded and released unharmed.

claims.paraphrase: When researchers walked across campus without equipment wearing the caveman mask, crows dive-bombed, scolded, and screamed alarms.
claims.printed_page_locator: Animal Behaviour 79(3), pp. 701-703, Results: Response to dangerous vs neutral masks
claims.support_summary: Masked walkers elicited harsh scolding and mobbing calls from resident crows, with birds swooping at the dangerous mask.

claims.paraphrase: When people walked across campus wearing a neutral politician mask, wild crows completely ignored them.
claims.printed_page_locator: Animal Behaviour 79(3), p. 702, Fig. 2: Percent mobbing encounters
claims.support_summary: Neutral control mask provoked almost zero response, proving specific facial recognition rather than general human aversion.

claims.paraphrase: Over five years, forty-seven crows mobbed the caveman mask, including fledglings born years after the initial test, because parents taught flockmates and offspring.
claims.printed_page_locator: Animal Behaviour 79(3), pp. 703-705, Results: Multi-year horizontal and vertical transmission
claims.support_summary: The percentage of birds scolding increased dramatically from 7 initial captures to 47 mobbing birds 5 years later, driven by social transmission.

editorial_suggestions.text: Open directly on the contrast of 7 trapped birds vs 47 birds mobbing 5 years later to maximize curiosity and retention.
Close with a conversational prompt to subscribe before crossing a crow, bridging directly into the replay loop.

dossier.protagonist: a Seattle wildlife researcher in a canvas jacket holding a rubber caveman mask

primary_source.title: Lasting recognition of threatening people by wild American crows

dossier.experiment_design: Field trials on a Seattle university campus where researchers wearing a rubber caveman mask captured and banded 7 crows, then recorded mobbing response rates from wild and naive crows over 5 years.
dossier.comparison_text: seven wild crows remembered the threatening caveman face and taught forty-seven birds to mob it across five years
dossier.broken_assumption: You think wild birds have simple, fleeting memory—until seven crows recognize your face and forty-seven attack five years later.
dossier.biological_mechanism: The crows used social learning and alarm calls to spread the threatening face to crows that never witnessed the original capture.
dossier.real_world_tax: Underestimating the social intelligence and observational memory of the creatures living quietly around you.
dossier.willpower_trap: Assuming human actions pass unnoticed by nature.
dossier.five_second_override: Respect the wild minds watching from the wires. Hit subscribe to learn more hidden wonders of the natural world.
dossier.best_hook: If you trap seven crows in a rubber mask, why did forty-seven wild birds attack that face five years later?
dossier.loop_bridge: Because the moment a crow marks you as an enemy...
